title: Compostable versus recyclable packaging: what each label means
subtitle: Understanding industrially compostable, home compostable, and recyclable claims before you put packaging in the wrong bin
excerpt: Compostable and recyclable packaging are often confused. 'Industrially compostable' requires an industrial composting facility at 60°C; it does not break down in a home compost bin and is not accepted in most kerbside recycling. 'Home compostable' will break down in a garden heap. 'Recyclable' means it can enter the kerbside recycling stream if accepted by your local authority.
sourceNotes: WRAP (Waste and Resources Action Programme) on compostable packaging in the UK (2023). European standard EN 13432 for industrial compostable packaging certification. AS 5810 (home compostable standard, adopted by some UK certifiers). OPRL (On-Pack Recycling Label) scheme guidance for UK retailers on recyclability claims.

glossaryTerms.definition: A material certified to break down completely at 60°C within 12 weeks in an industrial composting facility. It does NOT break down reliably in a home compost heap or in the environment.
A material certified to break down completely in a home compost heap at ambient temperature within 6 to 12 months. Certified to standards such as AS 5810 or TÜV Home Compostable.

content.text: The UK has no consistent system for collecting
industrially compostable
packaging from households. Most kerbside food waste collections exclude it: bioplastic contamination disrupts composting plants. Without a collection route, it ends up in residual waste.
What the labels mean
Industrially compostable (EN 13432):

breaks down at 60°C in 12 weeks. Requires an industrial facility. Does not break down in a home heap, a garden, or the ocean. Goes in residual waste in the UK unless your local authority specifies otherwise.
Home compostable:

breaks down in a garden compost heap at ambient temperature in 6 to 12 months. Certifications include AS 5810 (Australian) and TÜV Home Compostable. Add to the home compost heap. Do NOT add to kerbside recycling.
Recyclable (OPRL label):

can go in the kerbside recycling bin if accepted in your local authority area. OPRL rates recyclability as 'Recycle' (widely collected), 'Check locally', or 'Don't recycle yet'. The label does not guarantee your specific council collects it.
Biodegradable (no standard):
means nothing specific in UK or EU law. This term without a recognised certification standard (EN 13432, AS 5810) gives no information about where or how quickly the material breaks down.
Where each type goes
Industrially compostable packaging → residual waste bin. Local collection routes exist but are rare in the UK.
Home compostable
packaging → garden compost heap.
Recyclable plastic (OPRL 'Recycle') → kerbside recycling, if clean and dry.
Glass, steel, and aluminium → kerbside recycling, always.
Checking your local authority's accepted materials

Use the Recycle Now postcode checker (recyclenow.com) to find what your council accepts. Materials vary: some councils collect flexible film, others do not. Your own council's guidance takes priority over national guidance.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: Packaging marked 'compostable' has sat in the home compost heap for 6 months and has not broken down
rows.cause: The packaging is certified to EN 13432 (industrial compostable) rather than a home compostable standard; home heaps do not reach the temperatures required
rows.fix: Remove it and place it in the residual waste bin. Check the label for the specific certification standard. Only packaging certified to AS 5810 or TÜV Home Compostable will break down in a garden heap.
